rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch tethered to reportable banking questions and names the proof that would make or break each one. Its 'Mercury opens consumer accounts to customers it doesn't hold deposits for' has a specific desk, a real structural tension, and a useful kill condition. B has bones, but 'Two Years After SVB' is calendar-wrong and 'It Just Started Pitching Them Personally' turns a plausible sales motion into a fact. That is how a decent angle set talks itself into a correction.
gaps_in_A: 'The startup bank that grew on SVB's collapse now wants your paycheck' overreaches; checking and savings do not prove payroll or direct deposit intent.
'the same arrangement that has been the live question in fintech-banking supervision' imports an outside regulatory context without a supplied peg or citation.

'the first time the SVB-era customer base is being asked to bring their personal money too' assumes the invite pool is existing Mercury business customers; the update only says invite-only with a waitlist.

'Mercury picks a fight with neobanks and big banks at the same time' is viable but underpowered until Mercury discloses features, rates, fees, or terms that make the fight more than geography on a market map.
gaps_in_B: 'Two Years After SVB' is wrong; by June 9, 2026, SVB's March 2023 collapse is more than three years old. That is not a nuance, that is a preventable faceplant.
'Mercury's name recognition was built entirely on being the startup-banking alternative' overstates the supplied fact, which only says Mercury became well known after SVB.
'Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally.' invents a cross-sell motion; the facts do not say Mercury is pitching those business customers or their founders.

'Mercury's playbook runs opposite to the consumer-to-business neobank trajectory most competitors have tried' is unsupported market history; the set admits it needs comparables, so the thesis outruns the evidence.
